political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.
political.representative_figures_and_works: Ranke is one major nineteenth-century root. Later examples: Lewis Namier, Charles Tilly, and Lynn Hunt’s Politics, Culture, and Class (1984). Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.
strands.works: Vernon, Politics and the People (1993), ed., Re-reading the Constitution (1996); Epstein, Radical Expression (1994); Lawrence and Taylor, eds, Party, State and Society (1997); Lawrence, Speaking for the People (1998), Electing Our Masters (2009), 'Paternalism, Class, and the British Path to Modernity' (2011); Vernon's review and Lawrence's response (Reviews in History, 1999/2010)

nationalismstudies.label: Nationalism studies
nationalismstudies.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.
intellectualhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Arthur O. Lovejoy: The Great Chain of Being (1936); Quentin Skinner: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); J. G. A. Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

history_of_emotions.label: History of emotions
history_of_emotions.date_label: Earlier programme 1941 · Reddy’s framework 2001 · Rosenwein’s essay 2002 and book 2006 · methods discussion 2010
history_of_emotions.description: Emotions become objects and resources of historical inquiry: their valuations, expression and relation to action require evidence rather than an assumption of timeless feeling. Reddy’s emotives and emotional regimes connect expression, experience and enforced norms. Rosenwein’s emotional communities emphasize overlapping groups and movement between them. Their disagreement about political scale remains visible. Earlier programmes, including Febvre’s 1941 call, are resources to examine critically; the selected later works neither found nor delimit the whole field.
history_of_emotions.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier programme: Lucien Febvre, “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941; reprinted in Combats pour l’histoire, 1953). Selected frameworks: William M. Reddy, The Navigation of Feeling: A Framework for the History of Emotions (2001); Barbara H. Rosenwein, “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007). Named interlocutor: Norbert Elias, The Civilizing Process (1939), through Rosenwein’s 2002 criticism. Retrospective discussion: Jan Plamper’s interview with Reddy, Rosenwein and Peter Stearns (2010); only the specified Reddy/Rosenwein answers were read here.
history_of_emotions.scope_note: A bounded field entry distinguishing selected approaches, not a unified school or a census of its practitioners. Period 4 places the selected 2001–2010 interventions for teaching; the 1941 programme is an earlier root, not a founding date. Primary reading: Reddy’s 2001 publisher preface ix–xiii; Rosenwein’s 2002 essay, 821–822, 826–828 and 842–845; selected own answers in Plamper’s 2010 interview, Reddy 237–243 and Rosenwein 255–256. Existing Febvre reading qualifications remain. Rosenwein’s 2006 book is bibliographically checked but unread. The entry keeps political norms, overlapping communities and the interpretation of representations distinct. Later emotional-practice approaches, the full Stearns emotionology programme, sensory history and Sara Ahmed’s related affect inquiry require separate research; they are not silently equated with these frameworks. Review coverage retains the ordinary 2000 baseline; the selected 2001–2010 interventions do not extend it. No comprehensive review of later or non-European traditions is asserted. Dissertation counts guided discovery only and establish no relationship, agreement or field origin.

strands.title: Earlier programmes and their assumptions
strands.focus: Febvre’s call makes feelings part of historical explanation. Rosenwein’s retrospective also questions his separation of emotional and intellectual life; an earlier resource need not supply the later method unchanged.
strands.works: Febvre (1941); Rosenwein (2002), 821–822

strands.title: Emotives and enforced emotional norms
strands.focus: Reddy treats speaking about feeling as an intervention that may alter experience or expose an unexpected response. Regimes concern sanctions and conformity as well as shared styles; his 2010 account permits several within a wider polity.
strands.works: The Navigation of Feeling (2001), preface ix–xiii; Reddy in Plamper (2010), 240–243

strands.title: Communities, movement and source interpretation
strands.focus: Rosenwein studies emotional valuations and expected expressions across overlapping social groups. Movement between settings matters. Her Gregory of Tours example examines an author’s emotional representation without assuming the narrated conversation actually occurred.
strands.works: “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), 842–845; Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006), metadata only

strands.title: Against one progressive-restraint narrative
strands.focus: Rosenwein challenges an Elias-associated account that makes medieval emotion unrestrained and modernity controlled. Her alternative follows changing communities and relations between them; the critique does not make historical variation itself disappear.

strands.title: Regimes and communities: a disagreement with qualifications
strands.focus: Rosenwein objects to a dominant regime/refuge binary; Reddy explicitly accepts plural regimes and emphasizes enforceable norms. These positions partly overlap but are not interchangeable, and neither is an editorially settled theory.
strands.works: Answers in Plamper’s interview (2010): Reddy 243; Rosenwein 255–256
